title: How to Connect Python to MariaDB Database: Complete Guide
summary: Mito is AI for your Jupyter Notebook workflow. Use the Jupyter Agent, SQL, Database Connections, and Streamlit Apps for EDA and automations.
body_text:
See more blogs How to Connect Python to MariaDB Database: Complete Guide The Mito Team 10/6/2025 8 min read Turn data into insights and reports 4x faster with Mito AI Download Mito MariaDB is a popular open-source relational database management system that serves as a drop-in replacement for MySQL with additional features and performance improvements. When combined with Python, MariaDB provides a powerful platform for building robust, scalable applications. This comprehensive guide covers everything you need to know about connecting Python to MariaDB. Why Use MariaDB with Python? MariaDB with Python offers powerful capabilities: Drop-in replacement for MySQL with better performance Open-source with no licensing concerns Advanced storage engines (Aria, ColumnStore) Better query optimization and execution Enhanced replication features JSON support and dynamic columns Active community development Excellent compatibility with MySQL tools Prerequisites Before connecting Python to MariaDB, ensure you have: Python 3.6 or higher installed MariaDB server installed and running Database credentials (host, port, username, password, database) Basic understanding of Python and SQL Installing the MariaDB Connector The official MariaDB connector for Python provides optimal performance: bash pip install mariadb Alternatively, you can use the MySQL connector which is compatible: bash pip install mysql-connector-python We'll primarily use the official MariaDB connector in this guide. Basic Connection to MariaDB Let's start with a simple connection: python import mariadb import sys try: # Connect to MariaDB connection = mariadb.connect( user="your_username", password="your_password", host="localhost", port=3306, database="your_database" ) print("Connected to MariaDB successfully!") print(f"MariaDB version: {connection.server_version}") # Close connection connection.close() except mariadb.Error as e: print(f"Error connecting to MariaDB: {e}") sys.exit(1) Connection with Configuration Dictionary python import mariadb # Connection configuration config = { 'host': 'localhost', 'port': 3306, 'user': 'your_username', 'password': 'your_password', 'database': 'your_database' } try: connection = mariadb.connect(**config) print("Connected to MariaDB!") connection.close() except mariadb.Error as e: print(f"Error: {e}") Connection with Error Handling and Pooling python import mariadb from mariadb import Error def create_connection(): try: connection = mariadb.connect( user="your_username", password="your_password", host="localhost", port=3306, database="your_database", autocommit=False, connect_timeout=10 ) print("Successfully connected to MariaDB") # Get server info cursor = connection.cursor() cursor.execute("SELECT VERSION()") version = cursor.fetchone()[0] print(f"MariaDB version: {version}") cursor.close() return connection except Error as e: print(f"Error connecting to MariaDB: {e}") return None # Usage conn = create_connection() if conn: conn.close() Creating Tables python import mariadb connection = mariadb.connect( user="your_username", password="your_password", host="localhost", database="your_database" ) cursor = connection.cursor() # Create employees table create_table_query = """ CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS employees ( id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, first_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, last_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE, department VARCHAR(50), salary DECIMAL(10, 2), hire_date DATE, created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ) ENGINE=InnoDB """ cursor.execute(create_table_query) connection.commit() print("Table created successfully!") cursor.close() connection.close() Inserting Data Insert Single Record python import mariadb from datetime import date connection = mariadb.connect( user="your_username", password="your_password", host="localhost", database="your_database" ) cursor = connection.cursor() # Insert single employee insert_query = """ INSERT INTO employees (first_name, last_name, email, department, salary, hire_date) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?) """ employee_data = ('John', 'Doe', 'john.doe@company.com', 'Engineering', 75000.00, date.today()) cursor.execute(insert_query, employee_data) connection.commit() print(f"Employee inserted with ID: {cursor.lastrowid}") cursor.close() connection.close() Bulk Insert Operations python import mariadb connection = mariadb.connect( user="your_username", password="your_password", host="localhost", database="your_database" ) cursor = connection.cursor() insert_query = """ INSERT INTO employees (first_name, last_name, email, department, salary) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?) """ employees_data = [ ('Jane', 'Smith', 'jane@company.com', 'Marketing', 68000.00), ('Bob', 'Johnson', 'bob@company.com', 'Sales', 72000.00), ('Alice', 'Williams', 'alice@company.com', 'Engineering', 80000.00), ('Charlie', 'Brown', 'charlie@company.com', 'HR', 62000.00) ] cursor.executemany(insert_query, employees_data) connection.commit() print(f"{cursor.rowcount} employees inserted successfully!") cursor.close() connection.close() Querying Data Fetch All Records python import mariadb connection = mariadb.connect( user="your_username", password="your_password", host="localhost", database="your_database" ) cursor = connection.cursor() # Select all employees select_query = "SELECT id, first_name, last_name, department, salary FROM employees" cursor.execute(select_query) rows = cursor.fetchall() print(f"Total employees: {len(rows)}
") for row in rows: print(f"ID: {row[0]}, Name: {row[1]} {row[2]}, Dept: {row[3]}, Salary: ${row[4]}") cursor.close() connection.close() Fetch with Dictionary Cursor python import mariadb connection = mariadb.connect( user="your_username", password="your_password", host="localhost", database="your_database" ) cursor = connection.cursor(dictionary=True) # Query with dictionary access select_query = "SELECT * FROM employees WHERE department = ?" cursor.execute(select_query, ('Engineering',)) employees = cursor.fetchall() for emp in employees: print(f"Name: {emp['first_name']} {emp['last_name']}, Salary: ${emp['salary']}") cursor.close() connection.close() Parameterized Queries python import mariadb connection = mariadb.connect( user="your_username", password="your_password", host="localhost", database="your_database" ) cursor = connection.cursor() # Safe parameterized query select_query = "SELECT * FROM employees WHERE salary BETWEEN ? AND ?" cursor.execute(select_query, (70000, 80000)) employees = cursor.fetchall() print("Employees with salary $70k-$80k:") for emp in employees: print(f"{emp[1]} {emp[2]} - ${emp[5]}") cursor.close() connection.close() Updating Records python import mariadb connection = mariadb.connect( user="your_username", password="your_password", host="localhost", database="your_database" ) cursor = connection.cursor() # Update employee salary update_query = "UPDATE employees SET salary = ? WHERE id = ?" cursor.execute(update_query, (85000.00, 1)) connection.commit() print(f"{cursor.rowcount} record(s) updated") # Update multiple employees update_query = "UPDATE employees SET salary = salary * 1.10 WHERE department = ?" cursor.execute(update_query, ('Engineering',)) connection.commit() print(f"{cursor.rowcount} Engineering employees received raises") cursor.close() connection.close() Deleting Records python import mariadb connection = mariadb.connect( user="your_username", password="your_password", host="localhost", database="your_database" ) cursor = connection.cursor() # Delete employee by ID delete_query = "DELETE FROM employees WHERE id = ?" cursor.execute(delete_query, (10,)) connection.commit() print(f"{cursor.rowcount} record(s) deleted") cursor.close() connection.close() Working with Transactions python import mariadb connection = mariadb.connect( user="your_username", password="your_password", host="localhost", database="your_database", autocommit=False ) cursor = connection.cursor() try: # Start transaction cursor.execute("UPDATE employees SET salary = salary - 5000 WHERE id = 1") cursor.execute("UPDATE employees SET salary = salary + 5000 WHERE id = 2") # Commit transaction connection.commit() print("Transaction completed successfully") except mariadb.Error as e: # Rollback on error connection.rollback() print(f"Transaction failed: {e}") finally: cursor.close() connection.close() Using Stored Procedures python import mariadb connection = mariadb.connect( user="your_username", password="your_password", host="localhost", database="your_database" ) cursor = connection.cursor() # Create stored procedure proc_sql = """ CREATE PROCEDURE IF NOT EXISTS GetEmployeesByDepartment( IN dept_name VARCHAR(50) ) BEGIN SELECT * FROM employees WHERE department = dept_name ORDER BY last_name; END """ cursor.execute(proc_sql) connection.commit() # Call stored procedure cursor.callproc('GetEmployeesByDepartment', ['Engineering']) # Fetch results for result in cursor.stored_results(): employees = result.fetchall() print(f"Found {len(employees)} engineers") for emp in employees: print(f"{emp[1]} {emp[2]}") cursor.close() connection.close() Working with JSON Columns MariaDB supports JSON data type: python import mariadb import json connection = mariadb.connect( user="your_username", password="your_password", host="localhost", database="your_database" ) cursor = connection.cursor() # Create table with JSON column cursor.execute(""" CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS employee_metadata ( employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY, preferences JSON, skills JSON ) """) # Insert JSON data preferences = {"theme": "dark", "notifications": True, "language": "en"} skills = ["Python", "SQL", "Docker"] cursor.execute(""" INSERT INTO employee_metadata (employee_id, preferences, skills) VALUES (?, ?, ?) """, (1, json.dumps(preferences), json.dumps(skills))) connection.commit() # Query JSON data cursor.execute("SELECT preferences, skills FROM employee_metadata WHERE employee_id = 1") row = cursor.fetchone() prefs = json.loads(row[0]) emp_skills = json.loads(row[1]) print(f"Theme: {prefs['theme']}") print(f"Skills: {', '.join(emp_skills)}") # Query using JSON functions cursor.execute(""" SELECT JSON_EXTRACT(preferences, '$.theme') as theme FROM employee_metadata WHERE employee_id = 1 """) theme = cursor.fetchone()[0] print(f"Theme from JSON_EXTRACT: {theme}") cursor.close() connection.close() Connection Pooling python import mariadb # Create connection pool pool = mariadb.ConnectionPool( pool_name="my_pool", pool_size=5, pool_reset_connection=True, user="your_username", password="your_password", host="localhost", database="your_database" ) print(f"Connection pool created with {pool.pool_size} connections") # Get connection from pool connection = pool.get_connection() cursor = connection.cursor() cursor.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees") count = cursor.fetchone()[0] print(f"Total employees: {count}") cursor.close() connection.close() # Returns connection to pool Using Context Managers python import mariadb from contextlib import closing def get_connection(): return mariadb.connect( user="your_username", password="your_password", host="localhost", database="your_database" ) # Using context manager with closing(get_connection()) as conn: with closing(conn.cursor(dictionary=True)) as cursor: cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM employees WHERE salary > ?", (70000,)) employees = cursor.fetchall() for emp in employees: print(f"{emp['first_name']} {emp['last_name']} - ${emp['salary']}") Working with Dynamic Columns MariaDB's dynamic columns allow flexible schema: python import mariadb connection = mariadb.connect( user="your_username", password="your_password", host="localhost", database="your_database" ) cursor = connection.cursor() # Create table with dynamic column cursor.execute(""" CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS employee_extras ( employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY, extra_data BLOB ) """) # Insert dynamic column data cursor.execute(""" INSERT INTO employee_extras (employee_id, extra_data) VALUES (?, COLUMN_CREATE('certifications', 'AWS,Azure', 'languages', 'English,Spanish')) """, (1,)) connection.commit() # Query dynamic column cursor.execute(""" SELECT COLUMN_GET(extra_data, 'certifications' AS CHAR) as certs, COLUMN_GET(extra_data, 'languages' AS CHAR) as langs FROM employee_extras WHERE employee_id = 1 """) row = cursor.fetchone() print(f"Certifications: {row[0]}") print(f"Languages: {row[1]}") cursor.close() connection.close() Batch Processing python import mariadb connection = mariadb.connect( user="your_username", password="your_password", host="localhost", database="your_database" ) cursor = connection.cursor() # Prepare data for batch insert employees = [] for i in range(1000): employees.append(( f'FirstName{i}', f'LastName{i}', f'email{i}@company.com', 'Engineering', 70000 + (i * 100) )) # Batch insert insert_query = """ INSERT INTO employees (first_name, last_name, email, department, salary) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?) """ cursor.executemany(insert_query, employees) connection.commit() print(f"Batch inserted {cursor.rowcount} employees") cursor.close() connection.close() Complete Application Example python import mariadb import sys from contextlib import closing from datetime import date class EmployeeDatabase: def __init__(self, host, user, password, database): self.config = { 'host': host, 'user': user, 'password': password, 'database': database, 'autocommit': False } self.pool = self._create_pool() def _create_pool(self): try: return mariadb.ConnectionPool( pool_name="employee_pool", pool_size=5, **self.config ) except mariadb.Error as e: print(f"Error creating pool: {e}") sys.exit(1) def get_connection(self): return self.pool.get_connection() def create_employee(self, first_name, last_name, email, department, salary): with closing(self.get_connection()) as conn: with closing(conn.cursor()) as cursor: query = """ INSERT INTO employees (first_name, last_name, email, department, salary, hire_date) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?) """ cursor.execute(query, (first_name, last_name, email, department, salary, date.today())) conn.commit() return cursor.lastrowid def get_employee(self, employee_id): with closing(self.get_connection()) as conn: with closing(conn.cursor(dictionary=True)) as cursor: cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM employees WHERE id = ?", (employee_id,)) return cursor.fetchone() def get_employees_by_department(self, department): with closing(self.get_connection()) as conn: with closing(conn.cursor(dictionary=True)) as cursor: cursor.execute( "SELECT * FROM employees WHERE department = ? ORDER BY last_name", (department,) ) return cursor.fetchall() def update_salary(self, employee_id, new_salary): with closing(self.get_connection()) as conn: with closing(conn.cursor()) as cursor: cursor.execute( "UPDATE employees SET salary = ? WHERE id = ?", (new_salary, employee_id) ) conn.commit() return cursor.rowcount def delete_employee(self, employee_id): with closing(self.get_connection()) as conn: with closing(conn.cursor()) as cursor: cursor.execute("DELETE FROM employees WHERE id = ?", (employee_id,)) conn.commit() return cursor.rowcount def get_department_statistics(self): with closing(self.get_connection()) as conn: with closing(conn.cursor(dictionary=True)) as cursor: cursor.execute(""" SELECT department, COUNT(*) as employee_count, AVG(salary) as avg_salary, MIN(salary) as min_salary, MAX(salary) as max_salary FROM employees GROUP BY department ORDER BY employee_count DESC """) return cursor.fetchall() def search_employees(self, search_term): with closing(self.get_connection()) as conn: with closing(conn.cursor(dictionary=True)) as cursor: query = """ SELECT * FROM employees WHERE first_name LIKE ? OR last_name LIKE ? OR email LIKE ? """ search_pattern = f'%{search_term}%' cursor.execute(query, (search_pattern, search_pattern, search_pattern)) return cursor.fetchall() # Usage db = EmployeeDatabase( host='localhost', user='your_username', password='your_password', database='your_database' ) # Create employee emp_id = db.create_employee('Sarah', 'Connor', 'sarah@company.com', 'Security', 78000) print(f"Created employee with ID: {emp_id}") # Get employee employee = db.get_employee(emp_id) print(f"Employee: {employee['first_name']} {employee['last_name']}") # Get employees by department engineers = db.get_employees_by_department('Engineering') print(f"Found {len(engineers)} engineers") # Update salary rows_updated = db.update_salary(emp_id, 82000) print(f"Updated {rows_updated} employee(s)") # Get statistics stats = db.get_department_statistics() for stat in stats: print(f"

title: Improving Business Survey Targeting Through AI. Our Role in the UK Business Data Survey.
summary: The UK Business Data Survey 2024, commissioned by the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) and delivered by Ipsos , sought to better understand how UK businesses collect, use, store, and transfer data. A key challenge in this wave of the survey was identifying and reaching
body_text: The UK Business Data Survey 2024, commissioned by the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) and delivered by Ipsos , sought to better understand how UK businesses collect, use, store, and transfer data. A key challenge in this wave of the survey was identifying and reaching businesses involved in international data transfers — a relatively small and hard-to-locate subset of UK firms. To support this effort, DSIT and Ipsos engaged Glass.AI to provide an additional, targeted business sample. This involved using our automated web analysis to identify relevant firms based on open data signals. AI-Assisted Sample Construction At the start, Glass.AI confirmed with Ipsos the definition of ‘international data transfer’. It was suggested that the transfer of data to another country could be both internal and external, including UK businesses with operations abroad or UK subsidiaries of overseas companies. Then the first step in our process was to deep-read the UK web to build an initial dataset of potential candidates. The crawler looked for UK businesses that showed the following signals or indicators: ▪ Does the company have offices abroad? ▪ Does the company have people/employees abroad? ▪ Does the company mention international trade/activities on the website (e.g., press releases, mentions of foreign clients, partners, suppliers, JVs, etc.)? Glass.AI applied its large-scale language processing and web data analysis to scan over 2.2 million UK company websites, along with other digital content, to identify businesses likely to transfer data internationally. The initial crawl resulted in 20,000 candidate companies with evidence and classified by sector, size, and location. After additional filtering and validation of the signals by our data scientists, the final sample had 13,000 firms, all matched to Companies House. The approach was designed to complement the traditional sampling method used in the main survey and explore whether AI-driven discovery could improve targeting effectiveness. Comparison of Results Compared to the main sample, the Glass.AI sample resulted in fewer unusable leads: 33% in the Glass.AI sample, compared to 61% in the main sample source from company databases — and a significantly higher eligibility rate, with 79% of leads found to be in scope compared to 59% for the main sample. This ultimately produced a higher response rate from contact attempts and increased survey completion. These results suggest that AI-assisted identification led to a more targeted and efficient survey sample, particularly for businesses engaged in complex or less-visible data practices. Role in the Survey The AI-generated sample helped improve coverage of an underrepresented group: businesses transferring data internationally. This provided valuable support to the research objectives and contributed to a more robust evidence base for policy development. While the study remains exploratory in its use of AI for business sampling, the results suggest that such methods can be a useful complement to traditional approaches, particularly when targeting specialised or low-incidence business populations. Read more about the survey here: https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/uk-business-data-survey-2024

title: Cemtrex's Vicon Secures Approximately $900,000 Order to Equip U.S. Corrections Facility End-to-End

body_text: Cemtrex's Vicon Secures Approximately $900,000 Order to Equip U.S. Corrections Facility End-to-End July 30, 2026 8:30am EDT Download as PDF Single-facility award covers the complete Vicon platform through a specialist detention integrator Hauppauge, NY, July 30, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Vicon Industries, a subsidiary of Cemtrex, Inc. (Nasdaq: CETX, CETXP), today announced a purchase order valued at approximately $900,000 to equip a U.S. corrections facility with a complete Vicon security platform. The order was placed by a systems integrator specializing in detention security, whose name, along with that of the end customer, is not being disclosed. The order includes a broad mix of Vicon surveillance hardware and software, including outdoor dome and box cameras, multi-sensor cameras, video management workstations and software, recording servers, PCs, housings, mounts, lenses, and related accessories. The order reflects continued demand for Vicon's established security solutions in environments where video coverage, reliability, and long-term platform support are essential. Corrections is among the most demanding markets in physical security. Systems run continuously for years in hardened environments, and downtime is not tolerated. Integrators who specialize in this market select platforms they are prepared to stand behind for the life of the facility, and they concentrate an entire facility on a single vendor only when they trust that vendor completely. Vicon has served corrections and detention customers for decades, and awards of this kind are how that standing is measured. "Sustainable improvement at Vicon comes from execution, customer by customer and order by order," said Saagar Govil, Chairman and CEO of Cemtrex. "When an integrator puts every camera, every server, and every screen in a facility on one platform, they are making a long-term commitment to that vendor — and specialists in this market do not make that commitment casually. We have spent the past several quarters rebuilding Vicon into a sharper, more disciplined business. This award is a tangible example of that effort and a reaffirmation that customers continue to choose Vicon for demanding security environments where the cost of failure is high and platform continuity matters." The order is expected to ship in the current fiscal quarter and follows the strengthening public-sector and institutional activity the Company described in its second-quarter results. About Cemtrex Cemtrex, Inc. (Nasdaq: CETX, CETXP) is a diversified industrial and technology company operating across the Security, Industrial, and Aerospace & Defense sectors. The Company's Security segment, led by Vicon Industries, provides advanced video management software, high-performance security cameras, and integrated surveillance solutions for enterprise, government, and critical infrastructure customers. Its Industrial segment, through Advanced Industrial Services (AIS), delivers specialized rigging, millwrighting, process piping, and equipment installation services to manufacturers nationwide. Cemtrex's Aerospace & Defense segment, anchored by Invocon, provides mission-critical engineering, instrumentation, and sensing solutions supporting aerospace, defense, and space-based programs. With a focus on disciplined execution and strategic growth, Cemtrex is committed to building durable businesses that enhance safety, reliability, and long-term value for its customers and shareholders. title: Best Drizly Alternative Options for Alcohol Delivery in 2026
summary: Drizly shut down, but great alcohol delivery apps stepped up. Compare the best Drizly alternative options for fast, reliable delivery in 2026.
body_text: Looking for a solid Drizly alternative now that the original app is gone? You’re not alone. Drizly made ordering wine, beer, and liquor online feel normal. Its closure left a real gap for millions of U.S. shoppers. The good news: the alcohol delivery space didn’t disappear with it. A handful of apps picked up right where Drizly left off. Some have even improved on the original formula. This blog will show you the top Drizly alternative apps available today. You’ll see what makes each one worth trying. You’ll also see how the alcohol delivery business has shifted since Drizly’s exit. Shoppers will know exactly which app fits their next order. Founders eyeing this space will see why now might be the smartest time to build. At its peak, Drizly connected shoppers to thousands of local liquor stores. It did this through one simple app. Losing that kind of scale overnight is unusual. It’s exactly why lifestyle outlets like InsideHook published their own alternative roundups within days of the closure news. So many people still search for a direct replacement. The apps below aren’t identical copies of Drizly. Together, though, they cover nearly everything it used to offer. TL;DR • Drizly shut down in March 2024 and was absorbed into Uber Eats, which is now the closest direct successor. • Top Drizly alternative apps include Uber Eats, Saucey, Instacart, Minibar Delivery, Gopuff, and Frootbat. • Choose based on your priority: speed (Gopuff, Saucey), bundling (Instacart), local-store feel (Minibar), or rare bottles (Frootbat). • Alcohol delivery still runs through a complex three-tier, state-by-state regulatory system. • Drizly’s exit created real opportunity for independent retailers and founders to launch their own branded apps. • Appscrip’s alcohol delivery software offers a compliant, ready-to-launch foundation for entrepreneurs entering the space. Top Drizly Alternative Apps to Try in 2026 Drizly shut down in March 2024. Uber decided to fold its alcohol marketplace directly into Uber Eats. That single move reshuffled the entire on-demand booze delivery category almost overnight. Shoppers didn’t lose access to alcohol delivery, though. They just had to find a new home for it. Here’s how the leading options stack up today. Uber Eats is the most direct successor to Drizly. It absorbed much of Drizly’s original retailer network. If you already order food through the app, adding wine to that same cart is genuinely convenient. Saucey keeps things simple. It offers a roughly 30-minute delivery window in major metro areas, though it skips pickup entirely. Instacart shines when you want to fold alcohol into your weekly grocery order. It’s one of the few options offering both delivery and curbside pickup. Minibar Delivery operates closest to how Drizly originally worked. It connects shoppers directly to local liquor stores for beer, wine, spirits, and party supplies. App Best For Typical Delivery Time Curbside Pickup Notable Strength Uber Eats Combining alcohol with food or groceries Under 1 hour No Deepest local retailer network Saucey Fast, no-frills orders ~30 minutes No Simple, minimalist ordering Instacart Bundling alcohol with a grocery run 1–2 hours Yes Home delivery and curbside both available Minibar Delivery A Drizly-like local liquor store experience Varies by market No Curated selection from independent shops Gopuff Ultra-fast, flat-fee delivery Under 30 minutes No Own micro-fulfillment centers Frootbat Rare, allocated, or collectible bottles Varies No Specialist inventory you won’t find elsewhere For speed above everything, Gopuff stocks its own inventory in micro-fulfillment centers. That setup keeps delivery windows tight and predictable. It also bundles alcohol with snacks, household items, and other essentials in one order. If you’re hunting a hard-to-find bourbon or a limited-release wine, Frootbat specializes in exactly that. It even offers guides on distillery history and tasting notes. Most of these apps overlap on the basics. Age verification at signup and ID checks at the door are standard across the board. Payment options are similar too, typically credit, debit, and digital wallets. Where they differ is depth of selection. Some are tied to one retailer, others pull from a whole network of stores. That distinction matters more than most shoppers realize when an order needs to arrive fast. How to Pick the Right Alcohol Delivery App for You With six solid options on the table, picking one can feel harder than it should. The truth is most shoppers don’t need to commit to a single app. Many people keep two or three installed. They choose based on what a specific order requires. Not every app fits every occasion, so match the tool to the moment: Need it in 30 minutes or less? Gopuff or Saucey are built for speed. Already grocery shopping? Instacart lets you add alcohol to the same cart. Chasing a rare or allocated bottle? Frootbat specializes in scarce inventory. Want the Drizly-like local store feel? Minibar Delivery is the closest match. Ordering food and drinks together? Uber Eats handles both in one app. Comparing prices across multiple local stores? Uber Eats and Instacart both pull from several retailers at once. Value a smaller, curated retailer feel? Minibar Delivery leans into that experience deliberately. A quick gut check helps too: are you optimizing for speed, selection, or price? Most shoppers only need to answer that one question before the right app becomes obvious. A recent hands-on comparison of wine delivery apps tested Uber Eats, DoorDash, Instacart, and Total Wine side by side. It reached a similar conclusion. No single app won across every category. The best pick depended entirely on what mattered most that day. What Changed in Alcohol Delivery Since Drizly Closed Drizly’s shutdown wasn’t really about alcohol delivery losing steam. Industry leaders at the time pointed to Uber’s own strategic priorities, not weakening demand. BevAlc e-commerce has kept growing since then. Multiple retailers moved quickly to fill the space Drizly left behind. What did shift is how fragmented the market became. Instead of one dominant app, shoppers now juggle several options depending on location and occasion. That fragmentation is partly a regulatory story. Alcohol delivery in the U.S. still runs through a three-tier distribution system. Every state layers its own rules on top of it. Factor What It Means for Delivery Apps Three-tier distribution Producers, distributors, and retailers must stay legally separate in most states State-by-state variation An app available in California may not operate the same way in Pennsylvania or Utah Age verification ID checks at signup and at the door are mandatory, not optional Control vs. open states Some states run alcohol sales through state-owned agencies, limiting app options This patchwork is exactly why no single app has replicated Drizly’s old scale. Building compliant, region-aware alcohol delivery software is genuinely harder than building a standard delivery app. That complexity keeps new entrants cautious. According to the National Alcohol Beverage Control Association , no single entity can typically operate in more than one tier. That structure has held steady since Prohibition ended, and it isn’t going anywhere soon. For any Drizly alternative to succeed long term, it has to work within that framework. There’s also a quieter shift worth noting. Curbside pickup has become a standard expectation, not a bonus feature. Shoppers who got used to curbside groceries during the pandemic now expect the same for alcohol. Apps that skip pickup, like Saucey, are becoming the exception rather than the rule. The Business Opportunity Behind Drizly’s Exit Here’s the part most shopper-focused roundups skip. Drizly’s closure created real whitespace for founders, not just confusion for consumers. The U.S. alcohol delivery market has kept expanding since. Competitive intelligence platform CB Insights tracks over a dozen active companies in this space now. They range from regional players like BevMo to niche specialists like Flaviar. All of them are competing for the audience Drizly once owned outright. That level of competition is a healthy sign for anyone building here, not a warning sign. A few dynamics make this a genuinely attractive niche right now: Independent liquor stores still lack strong direct-to-consumer tools of their own. Regional and multi-store operators want an alternative to handing margin over to Uber Eats or Instacart. Consumers have shown they’re comfortable ordering alcohol online, so the habit is already built. Compliance requirements, while complex, are well-documented and solvable with the right software foundation. Smaller, focused apps can still compete on curation and service, even against giants like Uber Eats. None of this means building an alcohol delivery app is simple. It means the demand is proven. The competitive field is also more open than it looks from the outside. Grocery chains, regional liquor store groups, and even individual retailers are all testing their own branded delivery experiences. Rather than paying commission to Uber Eats or Instacart indefinitely, many are choosing to own the customer relationship directly. That shift mirrors what happened in food delivery years ago. Restaurants started building their own ordering apps alongside third-party marketplaces. Building Your Own Alcohol Delivery App Like the Best of Them If Drizly’s exit taught the industry anything, it’s this: the gap between “market leader” and “gone in three years” can be surprisingly narrow. Retailers, distributors, and regional entrepreneurs are stepping into that gap now. Many are launching their own branded delivery apps instead of routing every order through a third-party marketplace. Appscrip’s purpose-built alcohol delivery software was designed around exactly that opportunity. It bakes in the compliance features that make or break an alcohol delivery business. Operators don’t have to reinvent the wheel on age verification or regional rules. A few features matter more than others when evaluating alcohol delivery software: Feature Why It Matters ID verification at signup and delivery Keeps orders compliant with age-restriction laws Configurable order limits by region Adapts to state-by-state quantity restrictions Self-pickup option Mirrors what shoppers already expect from apps like Instacart Real-time order tracking Matches the experience shoppers got used to with Uber Eats Multi-store support Lets independent retailers compete with larger platforms It’s worth revisiting how the originals handled these problems first. Looking back at Drizly’s original app experience is telling. From ID checks to scheduled delivery, much of today’s playbook traces straight back to its design. Similarly, a closer look at Minibar’s app shows how a smaller, retailer-first model can still compete with bigger platforms. This same on-demand logic extends well beyond alcohol. Appscrip’s hyperlocal delivery marketplace solutions apply the same real-time, multi-store approach to groceries and retail. For a regional liquor store chain or a new entrant, launching from a proven codebase cuts both time and risk. Operators can skip months of building age-verification workflows and dispatch logic from scratch. Instead, they customize an existing, field-tested platform. That approach shortens the path from idea to a live app shoppers can use. Final Thoughts on the Best Drizly Alternative for Your Needs There’s no single best Drizly alternative for everyone. Uber Eats wins on convenience. Gopuff and Saucey win on speed. Instacart wins on bundling, Minibar wins on that local-store feel, and Frootbat wins for rare finds. Pick based on what you’re actually optimizing for. For founders and retailers, the calculus looks different. Drizly’s shutdown didn’t shrink the alcohol delivery market. It just opened room for sharper, more focused players to move in. Whether you’re a single liquor store or a growing chain, the tools to compete are more accessible than ever. title: Small shifts. Big impact. The leadership choices that matter most in the age of AI
summary: There is no shortage of conversation about what AI can do. Every day brings a new headline, a new capability, a new prediction about how work will change.
body_text: People and Culture Small shifts. Big impact. The leadership choices that matter most in the age of AI There is no shortage of conversation about what AI can do. Every day brings a new headline, a new capability, a new prediction about how work will change. Jul 27, 2026 By Rob Kowalski After spending time with our Novartis Culture Leadership Advisory Board (C-LAB), a diverse group of thought leaders from science, business, academia and sport helping us shape our culture journey, I came away thinking about a different question: What do we want AI to do? And just as importantly, what should stay firmly in human hands? One theme kept resurfacing: as AI accelerates change, leadership becomes less about having all the answers and more about creating the conditions for people to lean into that change. Often, it's many small shifts over time that can have the biggest impact. Here are four that stood out to me. 1. From friction to flow When trying to solve a challenge, our first instinct is often to add rather than subtract. A new process. A new tool. A new initiative. But many of the conversations at C-LAB pointed in the opposite direction. Sometimes the most powerful shift is choosing what to stop. Reimagining work should start with removing friction, not adding complexity. It requires us to create focus, make priorities clearer, and stop work that no longer adds value. So, how do we identify what needs stopping? At Novartis, we believe the people closest to the work are best placed to improve it. That's why we invited colleagues across the company to share the frictions they face and their ideas for making work simpler, faster and more impactful. Listening to those ideas, and acting on them together, is how we'll create new ways of working that help us make the most of emerging technologies and deliver even greater impact for our people, our business and, ultimately, patients. We also recognize that people don't just need new technology. They need a clear picture of where they're headed and why it matters. Leadership today isn't about pretending to have every answer; it's about helping people make sense of change and creating enough clarity for teams to move forward confidently, even when parts of the path are still emerging. Sometimes the most powerful thing a leader can do is decide what not to do. See what happened when Deepak Bisht asked some of our C-LAB leaders what they are letting go of. Stop adding meetings to create more clarity and energy What if reimagining work starts with stopping? Not adding another meeting. Not creating another process. Not making teams move faster without helping them focus better. Watch the video 2. From control to trust When the world around us is changing fast, it can be tempting for leaders to tighten their grip on control. Yet our own experience shows that new ways of working only scale when people feel trusted to experiment, contribute ideas and challenge assumptions. Building trust isn't about lowering standards or reducing accountability. It's about creating the conditions where people feel confident taking ownership and trying new approaches. If we want to see real progress, we need to normalize intelligent failure. As a pharmaceutical company, innovation is our lifeblood. Meaningful innovation requires experimentation, and experimentation inevitably comes with failures along the way. The goal isn't to avoid failure at all costs, but to learn from it quickly. Leaders help make that possible by creating environments where people feel safe to share failures and turn setbacks into progress. How? By sharing their own failures and learning out loud, together. This is especially important as AI becomes more integrated into how we work. As technology helps us move faster, the leader’s role in creating space for dialogue, applying human judgement, critical thinking, and thoughtful decision-making becomes even more crucial. At the same time, unbossed leadership means recognizing that there isn't one right way to achieve an outcome. Rather than prescribing every step, a leader’s job is to create clarity on the destination, trust their teams, and empower them to find the best path forward. Hear C-LAB member and Olympic champion Dominique Gisin reflect on her own experience of moving from control to trust in this conversation with Sujata Vaidyanathan . Building trust in a diverse leadership culture Do I really know what success looks like? As leaders, we often act with the best intentions: sharing our experience, offering guidance, and helping others avoid mistakes. Watch the video 3. From knowing to learning The pace of change means expertise alone is no longer enough. The leaders who thrive won't necessarily be those with the most answers. They'll be the ones who help others learn, adapt and grow. At Novartis, we want our people to feel equipped for the future, not intimidated by it. We want them to understand where we're headed and how they can help shape what comes next. It's about equipping people to be part of the journey. This isn't about having every answer today. It's about building the confidence, skills and mindset to keep learning as the world changes around us. A world where curiosity becomes a strategic advantage and learning isn't a separate activity from work, but part of how work gets done. Hear how C-LAB members are helping teams learn faster together in this conversation hosted by Jose Marcilla . What helps leaders learn faster in a world that keeps changing? As AI reshapes how we work, our culture will be shaped by the small practices we repeat every day: the questions we ask, the room we create for learning, and the courage to move from certainty to curiosity. Watch the video 4. From individual effort to collective impact Finally, we explored how organizations need to normalize experimentation and make learning more visible. Not individual experimentation happening in isolated pockets, but shared learning that helps entire teams move forward together. “Experimentation" can mean very different things to different people. Simply saying "the future of work" doesn't mean we're all picturing the same future. That's why storytelling and role-modelling matter. Leaders need to help people understand not only where we're going, but what that future means in practice for them and their teams. That means answering two questions. First: Where are we headed together? And second: What does that mean for me and my team? People need both. They need a shared sense of purpose and possibility, but they also need practical examples they can connect to their own work. Helping people understand what the future means for them individually—and how their role interconnects with colleagues, teams and the broader organization—is what turns individual growth into collective impact. As AI and new technologies transform how work gets done, the opportunity isn't simply to make individuals more productive. It's to help teams learn faster, solve problems, and create greater impact together . The opportunity ahead When I reflect on our conversations at C-LAB, I'm optimistic. Not because we have everything figured out, but because the discussion wasn't focused on the next technology trend. It was focused on something deeper: how we create the conditions for people to thrive, learn and deliver meaningful impact in a rapidly changing world. As work evolves, culture and leadership remain two of our most powerful levers. The future will be shaped by leaders who create clarity where there is complexity, trust where there is uncertainty, and connection where there is change. None of us has a complete picture of what the future will look like. What matters is that we're willing to learn, adapt and shape it together. Because meaningful change rarely happens all at once. It happens through small shifts that build over time. One conversation. One new habit. One better question at a time. What’s one small shift you are experimenting with right now? Join the conversation on LinkedIn!

title: Best Social Listening Tools for Fashion Brands (Trends Move in 72 Hours)
summary: Fashion micro-trends can peak within 48-72 hours. Compare 9 social listening tools on video AI, dupe monitoring, and fashion-specific fit for 2026 buyers.
body_text: TL;DR: The best social listening tools for fashion brands in 2026 include Syncly Social for catching untagged trend and dupe conversation inside TikTok, Reels, and Shorts video; Meltwater and Brandwatch for enterprise fashion/retail teams that want dedicated fashion-industry reporting and named fashion customers; Talkwalker for non-gated speech-to-text and video/logo recognition without a full management suite; Sprinklr for large enterprises that want listening bundled inside a unified CX platform; and Brand24, Mention, YouScan, and Sprout Social for teams whose monitoring needs are genuinely general-purpose. Fashion is a vertical where micro-trends can peak in 48-72 hours, where the evidence of an emerging trend usually lives in video rather than in a caption, and where recurring reputational risk — counterfeit conversation, size-inclusivity backlash, greenwashing accusations — shows up in comment sections and GRWM videos long before it shows up in a keyword search. A TikTok haul video doesn't announce itself in the caption. Neither does the moment a creator holds up a dupe and says the real brand's name out loud, or the comment thread underneath a runway recap that turns into a size-inclusivity pile-on. By the time any of that is typed into a hashtag, the trend — or the crisis — is usually already past its peak. Most social listening tools were built to catch text: captions, hashtags, reviews. Fashion mostly happens somewhere else. Below are nine tools fashion marketers actually use to monitor trend velocity, dupe conversation, and reputational risk, graded honestly on which ones have real fashion-specific evidence behind them and which ones are simply good general-purpose options. Why does social listening matter differently for fashion brands than for other verticals? Fashion moves faster than a weekly reporting cadence can catch, and the earliest evidence of a trend is almost always visual or spoken rather than typed. Micro-trends on TikTok and Instagram can peak within 48-72 hours of gaining traction, and they typically crystallize once three to four mid-tier creators (50k-500k followers) converge on the same item or aesthetic and a hashtag finally forms (Source: Later, 2026 ). That timing matters: by the time a trend is searchable by hashtag volume, it's often already near its peak — see our deeper breakdown of fashion trend signals for more on how these cycles show up in the data. Trend-cycle velocity : the speed at which a fashion micro-trend moves from first appearance — a single creator's video — to peak visibility and saturation, often in as little as 48-72 hours on TikTok or Instagram. Detection has to happen before a hashtag crystallizes, not after. Most of that early evidence is buried in video, not text . TikTok video publishing rose 72% year-over-year in a sample of 2.3M+ posts across 92,000+ accounts, while image and carousel posts rose 140% — meaning the volume of content a caption-only tool has no way to parse is growing faster than the content it can actually read (Source: Metricool 2026 TikTok Study, via Draper ). AI computer-vision vendors have built entire forecasting businesses around this gap: Heuritech says it analyzes 3M+ social images daily across roughly 2,000 fashion attributes and claims to forecast trend growth up to 24 months ahead at over 90% accuracy, a service Louis Vuitton and Dior reportedly use for collection planning (Source: Heuritech, 2026 ) — treat that specific accuracy figure as a vendor-published claim rather than an independently audited one, but the underlying point holds: fashion trend signal lives in imagery and speech first. The vertical's recurring reputational risks follow the same pattern — they surface in conversation and video before they show up anywhere a keyword tool would catch them cleanly: Counterfeit and dupe conversation. Apparel is the single riskiest category Entrupy authenticates: 34.85% of submitted apparel items in 2025 couldn't be authenticated, versus 8.1% for luxury goods overall and 11.1% for footwear. Some specific labels — Fear of God Essentials (95.75%), BAPE (85.19%) — had counterfeit rates above 85% of submissions (Source: Entrupy — State of the Fake Report 2026 ). Worth being precise here: general social listening tools, Syncly Social included, are not counterfeit-detection or brand-protection products — that's a separate category built for takedowns and marketplace enforcement (think BrandShield, MarqVision, Red Points, or Entrupy itself). What listening legitimately offers is visibility into the conversation : volume, sentiment, which specific products are being called out. Size-inclusivity backlash. Vogue Business's Spring/Summer 2025 Size Inclusivity Report found 94.9% of runway looks were straight-size, with plus-size representation at just 0.8%. The Fall/Winter 2026 menswear edition found plus-size representation fell further still, to 0.2% of 2,523 looks across Milan and Paris, down from 0.3% the prior season (Source: MR Magazine, 2026 ). Brands that lead with "size-inclusive" messaging and then quietly narrow their in-store range — as Old Navy did after its 2021 BODEQUALITY commitment — tend to get called out for it in exactly the kind of comment-section conversation a listening tool is built to surface (Source: The Curvy Fashionista, 2026 ). Greenwashing accusations. Italy's competition authority fined Shein €1 million in August 2025 for misleading environmental claims, on top of an earlier €40 million fine from France (Source: Euronews, 2025 ). SKIMS scored zero out of 150 on the 2024 Remake Fashion Accountability Report, tied with Shein for the lowest possible score (Source: via itismandystyle, 2026 ). None of this shows up cleanly in NPS data or a monthly report. It shows up in a GRWM caption-free video, a comment thread, or a creator saying a competitor's name out loud — which is exactly the gap between tools that only parse text and tools built to catch what's said and shown. Which social listening platforms actually have fashion-specific positioning or fashion-brand use cases? Four vendors have real, current, fashion-specific evidence behind them — named customers, dedicated fashion pages, or fashion-industry reporting — and four have none at all, which is worth knowing honestly before you shortlist rather than discovering after a demo. Vendor Fashion-specific evidence found Assessment Syncly Social Fashion named explicitly as a target industry (alongside Beauty, F&B, Consumer goods); Audio Intelligence + AI Vision built to catch trend/dupe conversation inside video Fashion-specific by design, video-native Meltwater Dedicated "Retail & Fashion" page; named customers PUMA, H&M Mexico, Country Road Fashion-specific, current Brandwatch Dedicated Fashion Index + Retail industry page + recurring fashion-trend reports Fashion-specific, current — but image/video analysis is roadmapped, not yet shipped Talkwalker Dedicated Fashion & Beauty industry report Fashion-specific, current — video/audio AI described generically, not confirmed short-form-specific Sprinklr Own blog post analyzing Paris Fashion Week listening data; Prada Group case study Real evidence, but the Prada case is from 2020 (dated) and Sprinklr is enterprise-only since Self-Serve retired April 2026 Brand24 None found General fit, not fashion-specific — honest budget/text-first option YouScan None found (checked YouScan's own "social listening examples" directly — no fashion brand appears) General fit, not fashion-specific Sprout Social None found beyond a generic third-party industry tag General fit, not fashion-specific Mention None found General fit, not fashion-specific Meltwater has the clearest fashion footprint of the group: a dedicated "Meltwater for Fashion Brands" page naming PUMA, H&M Mexico, and Country Road as customers (Source: Meltwater — Retail & Fashion, 2026 ). Brandwatch runs a standing "Fashion" index for ongoing category benchmarking plus a separate retail industry page and recurring fashion-trend blog analysis (Source: Brandwatch — Fashion Index, 2026 ). Sprinklr has published its own social-listening breakdown of Paris Fashion Week conversation — dresses generated 26.7K mentions versus 19.3K for tops and shirts, a direct example of what its listening output looks like on fashion content (Source: Sprinklr, 2026 ). Talkwalker publishes a standing Fashion & Beauty industry report and Fashion Week trend-analysis content (Source: Talkwalker, 2026 ). Brand24, YouScan, Sprout Social, and Mention are legitimate tools at their respective price points, but none turned up a fashion-specific case study, named customer, or dedicated fashion page in this research — including a direct check of YouScan's own social-listening examples, which features McDonald's, Duolingo, and Stanley but no fashion brand. That's a fair thing to know before choosing one of them for a fashion use case specifically: they're general-fit options, not fashion specialists. How do the best social listening tools for fashion brands compare on pricing, video/audio AI, and fashion-specific fit? The vendors with real fashion evidence and genuine video-AI depth — Syncly Social and Meltwater — sit at the top for teams that need both. Brandwatch and Talkwalker offer strong fashion-adjacent content and enterprise breadth, but their video capabilities are either not yet shipped (Brandwatch) or described generically rather than confirmed for short-form video specifically (Talkwalker). Sprinklr is enterprise-only with real but dated fashion proof points. Brand24, Mention, YouScan, and Sprout Social are solid options at their price points with no confirmed fashion-specific positioning. See our guide on how to measure untagged mentions for more on why this matters. A caption-only listening tool can tell you a haul video got hashtagged #ootd. It can't tell you a creator named a specific dupe brand out loud, or that your product showed up on someone's dresser in the background of a GRWM with no caption at all — the exact gap covered in our breakdown of what short-form video misses . That's the gap Syncly Social's Audio Intelligence and AI Vision are built to close, using speech-to-text and visual detection across 10+ platforms so a mention doesn't need to be typed to be caught. That doesn't make it the only right answer, though: Meltwater and Brandwatch have real, current fashion-specific proof points of their own, and for a team that already needs enterprise benchmarking with a decade of historical archives or a dedicated fashion-industry account team, either is a legitimate choice. Talkwalker is worth a look for teams that want Blue Silk AI's non-gated speech-to-text and video/logo recognition without paying for Hootsuite's full publishing and management layer on top. Sprinklr fits large enterprises that specifically want listening folded into a broader unified customer-experience suite spanning care, marketing, and social — though it's worth knowing its clearest fashion proof point, the Prada Group deployment, dates to 2020. Brand24 and Mention remain honest, affordable choices for fashion teams whose monitoring needs are genuinely text- and caption-first; YouScan is a reasonable pick for visual-first brand-safety use cases like spotting a logo in someone's photo; and Sprout Social works well for teams that want publishing, scheduling, and listening bundled into one seat-based tool. None of the four has a confirmed fashion-specific case study, but that doesn't disqualify them — it just means the pitch for choosing them is general capability, not vertical fit. Key Takeaways Fashion micro-trends can peak within 48-72 hours of gaining traction, and by the time a trend is searchable by hashtag volume, it's often already near its peak (Later, 2026). Apparel has the highest counterfeit-authentication-failure rate of any category Entrupy tracks — 34.85% — but general social listening tools are visibility layers for dupe conversation, not counterfeit-detection or brand-protection products. Meltwater, Brandwatch, Sprinklr, and Talkwalker all have real, current fashion-specific evidence (named customers, dedicated fashion pages, or fashion-industry reports); Brand24, YouScan, Sprout Social, and Mention are honest general-fit options with no confirmed fashion-specific positioning. Size-inclusivity backlash and greenwashing accusations are recurring fashion reputational risks that surface in video and comment-section conversation before they show up in any keyword search. Video-native tools that catch untagged mentions — spoken or shown, never typed — have a structural advantage for fashion specifically, since so much of the vertical's trend and risk signal lives outside the caption. How should a fashion brand actually decide? Start from what you're actually trying to catch. If the priority is spotting a trend or a dupe callout before it's typed into a hashtag — the exact moment a caption-only tool misses entirely — Syncly Social is built for that specific gap, using audio and on-screen visual detection instead of relying on text matches. If your team already needs enterprise-scale benchmarking or competitive analysis with a named fashion account history, Meltwater and Brandwatch both bring real, current proof points to that conversation. If Blue Silk AI's non-gated video and speech capabilities without a full publishing suite fit your stack better, Talkwalker is worth a serious look. And if your monitoring needs are genuinely general-purpose rather than fashion-specific — competitor names, review sites, basic caption tracking — Brand24, Mention, YouScan, and Sprout Social remain honest, capable choices at their respective price points. title: GMP Basics and When FDA Expects Compliance: Enforcement Lessons
summary: What GMP requires, when FDA enforcement says it applies, and what early-stage manufacturers have actually been cited for.
body_text: What GMP is, and when it starts applying: lessons from FDA's enforcement record GMP in one paragraph Good manufacturing practice (GMP), which FDA calls current good manufacturing practice (CGMP), is the body of requirements that govern how a drug or biologic is made, tested, packaged, stored, and released so that each unit has the identity, strength, quality, and purity it is represented to have. For finished pharmaceuticals the core rules sit in 21 CFR Parts 210 and 211; for biologics they are layered with the Public Health Service (PHS) Act. The statutory hook is section 501(a)(2)(B) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic (FD&C) Act: a drug is deemed "adulterated" if the methods, facilities, or controls used to manufacture it do not conform to CGMP. FDA uses that exact formulation in enforcement letters, telling firms their product "is adulterated within the meaning of section 501(a)(2)(B)" whenever manufacturing controls fall short 124 128 136 . In practice GMP is less a checklist than a functioning quality system: a quality unit with real authority, controlled and validated processes, documented batch records, stability data, contamination control, and investigation of anything that goes wrong. The question that trips up early-stage companies: when does it start? The common assumption is that GMP is a commercial-launch problem: something you build out once an NDA or BLA is on the horizon. The enforcement record says otherwise. GMP obligations attach as soon as a product meets the statutory definition of a drug or biologic and is made for administration to humans, which includes material made for clinical investigation, well before any approval exists. The obligation is "phase-appropriate," meaning the depth of validation and control scales with the stage of development, but it is never zero. The EU frames the same principle explicitly, which is useful for contrast. EU GMP requires investigational medicinal products (IMPs) to be manufactured under GMP from the clinical-trial stage onward, with a quality system meant to protect trial subjects and preserve the reliability of clinical data, batch certification by a Qualified Person, and controls that are "flexible and appropriate to the stage of development" and become more defined as knowledge increases 48 49 50 52 54 57 . FDA's expectation is the same in substance: the earlier the phase, the more the controls are risk- and knowledge-based, but the foundational quality system must exist before you put product into a human. The clearest illustration of "GMP does not wait for approval" is how FDA treats products that never had approval at all. When a firm manufactures an unapproved or investigational drug or biologic and its controls are deficient, FDA does not excuse the deficiency because the product is pre-approval. It cites the product as adulterated under CGMP anyway. FDA applied section 501(a)(2)(B) to CGMP deficiencies at US Stem Cell Clinic, LLC 120 , and at Berkeley Biologics, LLC it stacked the citations: unapproved new drug/biologic under section 351(a)(1) of the PHS Act and section 505(a) of the FD&C Act, plus CGMP adulteration for the drug product 121 . The message is that being pre-approval is not a shield; it is often the reason FDA is looking. What FDA has actually cited early-stage and development-stage manufacturers for Cell, gene, and tissue products administered to patients before approval The richest set of examples comes from cell-therapy, tissue, and exosome firms whose products were being given to patients or studied clinically without the manufacturing foundation in place. These are the closest analogues to a modern early-stage biotech making its own clinical material. StemGenex Biologic Laboratories, LLC was cited for significant CGMP deviations in its stromal vascular fraction (SVF) product used in humans: unvalidated manufacturing processes, an uncontrolled environment, lack of control over components, and insufficient product testing, including sterility and endotoxin testing 67 . FDA specifically questioned whether each lot was tested for sterility and flagged that the endotoxin specification appeared to have been loosened after a validation failure, leaving results above acceptable limits for many patients 111 . TCA Cellular Therapy, LLC was cited for administering investigational products to patients not enrolled in the IND studies, using allogeneic cells where the protocol required autologous cells, treating patients while studies were on clinical hold, and donor-eligibility and communicable-disease testing failures. In specific instances a subject received the wrong investigational product and another received allogeneic donor cells instead of their own stem cells 77 . Safari Stem Cell, LLC was cited for lack of validated manufacturing processes, failure to perform sterility testing on batches of stem-cell product administered intravenously or intrathecally, and no environmental monitoring in the aseptic processing area 112 113 . EUCYT Laboratories LLC was cited for unvalidated aseptic processes for products including XOsomes and VidaStem, deficient environmental and personnel monitoring, inadequate control of incoming umbilical-cord components, and sterility failures that were not thoroughly investigated 114 . Dynamic Stem Cell Therapy and Supreme Rejuvenation, LLC were cited for marketing unapproved biologics (an umbilical-cord product and exosome products, respectively) with no IND and no BLA, against a backdrop of FDA safety concern after serious adverse events tied to exosome products 69 76 . The common thread is not exotic. These firms skipped the basics that GMP requires from the first human dose: a validated process, a controlled aseptic environment, sterility and endotoxin testing on every lot, component control, and real investigation of failures. Sterility and aseptic processing in clinical and small-batch sterile production Sterile products carry the highest patient risk, and FDA's Form 483 observations show the same aseptic deficiencies whether the site is a large manufacturer, a compounding pharmacy, or a 503B outsourcing facility. For any early-stage company making a sterile injectable for a trial, these are the recurring failure modes FDA documents: Media fills that do not simulate worst-case aseptic operations, including realistic staffing, unit counts, interventions, and batch size (cited at outsourcing and sterile-production facilities such as ProRx LLC, Nephron sterile compounding sites, AnazaoHealth, and Mandell's Clinical Pharmacy) 81 84 89 95 97 . Weak environmental and personnel monitoring: no monitoring during production, no dynamic (in-operation) sampling, inadequate glove monitoring, and action levels without justification 82 88 90 91 . Inadequate cleaning and disinfectant-efficacy validation, including failure to use a sporicidal agent and missing organisms or surfaces in efficacy studies 93 97 103 . Insufficient sterility and endotoxin testing of finished sterile product, with testing frequency and acceptance criteria never established (cited at Clinical Apothecaries and Pinnacle Compounding, among others) 86 88 93 . The foundational quality-system gaps small and new manufacturers repeat Across warning letters to small, new, or development-stage manufacturers, FDA cites the same structural absences, the systems a startup is tempted to defer: No adequate quality unit, or a quality unit with no written responsibilities and no real authority over release 24 25 30 33 34 37 39 40 43 . No stability program and no representative batches on stability, so shelf-life claims are unsupported 24 27 39 . No validated aseptic process and inadequate environmental controls 22 39 . Inadequate batch records, master production records, and complete laboratory data 23 26 31 33 35 36 37 40 41 43 . No process validation, change control, or written procedures 23 26 30 31 35 36 42 43 . Failure to investigate deviations, out-of-specification results, and complaints, with weak or absent CAPA 23 26 28 30 31 32 33 35 38 41 42 . Sanofi Pasteur, for example, was cited for aseptic process simulations that omitted pre-filtration and cleaning operations, an unvalidated microbiological method, and no integrity testing of sterile vent filters 22 . Stemell Inc was cited for no stability program, no calibrated or monitored cold storage, no complaint procedures, and no quality-control unit 39 . 483s tied directly to clinical trial material FDA investigators have also documented deficiencies that reach the clinical-supply chain specifically. Ohm Laboratories, Inc. was cited when a validation batch of Oxcarbazepine Suspension was converted to a trial batch despite prior failed validation batches, with no documented transfer procedure, undocumented critical viscosity steps, operator-dependent manual additions, and no established process controls 14 . Beacon Hill Medical Pharmacy was cited for sterile-injectable component and closure controls: components not tested or released before use, missing identity and endotoxin testing, and no container-closure integrity testing 15 . These are the kinds of observations that surface when a company treats early batches as informal and only "gets serious" about controls later. The practical takeaway for regulatory and CMC teams GMP is not a launch milestone; it is a condition of putting product into a human. The controls are phase-appropriate, so a Phase 1 program is not held to the full commercial validation burden, but the enforcement record shows FDA expects the load-bearing elements to exist from the first clinical batch: an empowered quality unit, defined and controlled processes, complete batch records, stability data, contamination control for anything sterile, and genuine investigation of failures. The firms FDA cites are overwhelmingly those that treated these as post-approval concerns. For companies making their own clinical material, the pattern is a checklist of what to have in place before, not after, the first patient is dosed.

body_text: Animal welfare has moved from a niche concern to a defining factor in how consumers evaluate food. According to the Power of Meat 2025 study, 39% of consumers say label claims mentioning “humanely raised” influences their purchasing decisions. But as demand grows, so does the question: How do you know those claims are real? Verifying animal welfare practices ensure that claims about humane treatment are not just stated—but proven—through standards, audits, and additional oversight. What Are Animal Welfare Claims in Beef and Livestock? Animal welfare claims refer to verified declarations made by beef and livestock producers regarding the treatment of animals in their care. These claims typically encompass a variety of practices widely based on animal welfare frameworks, such as the Five Domains, used to assess, measure, and facilitate overall quality of life for animals. The Five Domains was the foundational standard that brings attention to animal welfare and management that is a subjective focus to an animal’s overall welfare state. The Five Domains: Nutrition Environment Health Behavior Mental State Photo Credit: https://www.researchgate.net/figure/The-Five-Domains-Model-modified-from-12-The-examples-provided-for-the_fig1_319020431 The Role of Low-Stress Handling Coinciding with the Five Domains, low-stress management practices play a critical role in animal welfare. They focus on minimizing fear and anxiety during an animal’s life from birth to harvest. Promoting the positive not only improves animal well-being but also greatly contributes to higher quality meat products and enhanced food safety, making it both an ethical and economic priority. It is imperative that producers take care of their animals, not only because they care about them, but because it impacts the quality of the product they are working so hard to produce. Why Animal Welfare Verification Matters Consumer Trust Consumers increasingly expect proof of ethical claims. Animal welfare verification becomes essential for building trust. Verification provides confidence that products meet standards backed by science. Retailer Requirements Many retailers are adopting stringent animal welfare policies, requiring suppliers to verify their claims. This demand for verified animal welfare practices helps ensure that products on store shelves meet standards that align with the values of socially conscious consumers. Risk Mitigation Verification of animal welfare claims helps mitigate risks associated with non-compliance. Producers who adhere to established standards reduce risks tied to: Mislabeling Greenwashing Negative publicity Regulatory exposure Differentiation in Market Verified animal welfare claims help brands stand out in crowded markets and can serve as a unique selling proposition for producers and brands. Consumers are willing to pay a premium for ethically produced protein products. Photo Credit: Power of Meat Study 2025 How Animal Welfare Is Verified Step-by-Step Verification Process The verification of animal welfare claims involves a systematic process that includes: Selecting a Standard A clear, measurable standard defines expectations around: Animal care Nutrition Health management Handling practices Traceability Desk or On-Farm Audits Auditors conduct on-site evaluations —often annually or unannounced—to assess real-world conditions. For animal welfare, physical observation is essential. You can’t verify animal care from paperwork alone. Documentation Review Producers must maintain records that demonstrate compliance, including: Health and treatment logs Feed and nutrition records Training documentation Corrective Actions If deficiencies are identified during audits, producers must implement corrective actions to address issues and improve animal welfare practices. Ongoing Monitoring Verification is continuous, not one time. Periodic reassessments, often annually, are crucial to maintaining compliance and ensuring that animal welfare practices evolve with industry standards and consumer expectations. What Happens During an Animal Welfare Audit? During an animal welfare audit, trained auditors assess various aspects of the livestock operation. Auditors evaluate: Animal caretaker training Animal behavior and health Facility conditions (space, shelter, access to food and water) Handling and transportation practices Veterinary care records Feed and water Etc. Auditors may also interview staff to ensure that welfare practices are understood and implemented consistently. Who Verifies Animal Welfare Claims? Government vs Third-Party Government agencies establish regulatory baselines Third-party organizations provide independent verification through audits Animal welfare claims can be verified by government agencies or independent third-party organizations. Government oversight typically involves regulations that producers must follow, while third-party verifiers provide an additional layer of credibility through external audits. Role of Independent Verifiers, Reviewers, and Auditors Independent verifiers play a crucial role in ensuring the integrity of animal welfare claims. They conduct audits, assess compliance with established standards, and issue certificates that validate adherence to humane practices. Working with a third-party verification organization can enhance a producer's credibility and build consumer trust. Organizations like Where Food Comes From conduct audits, assess compliance, and validate claims through structured verification programs. This third-party layer adds credibility and transparency beyond internal or regulatory checks. Common Misconceptions Despite growing awareness, several misconceptions persist regarding animal welfare claims: “All Labels Are Trustworthy” Not all animal welfare labels are created equal. Consumers should look for labels that are third-party certified from recognized organizations to ensure claims are verified and authentic. “Animal Welfare Is Just About Food” While nutrition is crucial, animal welfare encompasses a broader range of practices, including housing, treatment, and handling, as we mentioned above when we discussed The Five Freedoms. As well as promoting practices that align with sustainability goals that run up and down the supply chain. “Audits Happen Once” Understanding that animal welfare verification is an ongoing process is essential . Regular audits and continuous improvement are vital for maintaining compliance. How Retailers and Brands Use Verified Animal Welfare Claims Retailers and brands leverage verified animal welfare claims to enhance their market position. By promoting their commitment to humane treatment, verified animal welfare claims help brands: Build trust with consumers Meet retailer requirements Differentiate in competitive markets Reduce reputational risk The Future of Animal Welfare Verification Increased Transparency As consumers demand greater transparency regarding food production, the future of animal welfare verification will likely incorporate more data and traceability. This trend will help ensure that claims can be substantiated and that consumers can trace their food back to the farm o ranch of origin. Consumer Demand The growing consumer demand for ethically-produced food will continue to drive advancements in animal welfare verification. Producers who prioritize humane practices will likely find increased opportunity from buyers, brands and retailers that are looking to fill the demand from consumers who are willing to pay a premium for verified products. Data + Traceability Integration Integrating data and traceability into animal welfare verification processes can enhance accountability. FAQ Section What does an animal welfare certification mean? An animal welfare certification indicates that a livestock operation has met specific standards for humane treatment and care, verified through a third-party verification organization that works alongside independent auditors. Who verifies animal welfare in beef? Both government agencies and independent third-party organizations verify animal welfare claims in beef production, ensuring compliance with established standards. Consumers likely need to do some research to determine if the labels they see on packaging are a third-party verified claim. Are animal welfare claims regulated? Yes, animal welfare claims are regulated, but the level of regulation can vary by country and certification program. It's essential to look for recognized certifications for assurance. What is the difference between audited and certified? Audited refers to the producer’s practices having been evaluated against a set of standards, while certified means that a producer has successfully met those standards and received official recognition. Bottom Line Animal welfare verification transforms claims into proof. Through standards, audits, and continuous oversight, verification ensures that humane treatment is not just promised but practiced. As transparency becomes the expectation, verified animal welfare claims will play a defining role in the future of food.
